newsitem.title: CANADA: Methanex reviewing other methanol projects.
newsitem.headline: Methanex reviewing other methanol projects.

text.p: After failing in its quest to buy a Trinidad methanol plant, Methanex Corp said on Thursday that it is exploring alternative opportunities and has the means to fund US$350 million in other projects.

The world's biggest methanol producer negotiated for a year to acquire the 69 percent stake in Trinidad Tobago Methanol Co held by the Trinidad government. But a minority shareholder in the project exercised a right of first refusal and Methanex said it was abandoning the effort.
Pierre Choquette, Methanex chief executive, told a conference call the company had capacity beyond existing commitments to fund about US$350 million in new methanol projects.
Methanex is also generating "substantial" free cash flow, he said. "We have three or four other projects we are working on...We are talking to a number of people."
Methanex is looking at both buying existing facilities and building new ones, Choquette said. He declined to give details, saying the company would make an announcement if a deal solidified.
Among the three to four projects under consideration are opportunities to take an ownership stake in plants where Methanex already markets the production, he said.

Methanol is a chemical feedstock derived from natural gas that is used in a wide array of applications including building materials, paints, resins and as an additive to clean-burning gasoline. Demand for the commodity has traditionally been closely linked to the economic cycle.
NOVA Corp owns about 25 percent of Methanex.
Long term, Methanex is reviewing options for serving Asia, Choquette said.

Gas supply contracts for its existing New Zealand plants expire between 2003 and 2005 and the company is exploring possibilities to establish a strategic production "hub" in the region with competitively priced gas supply. This would be similar to the company's large complex in Chile which has the lowest production costs of all its plants.

"We continue to look at alternatives for New Zealand in the event we no longer have access to competitively priced gas. Where we might have another strategic type of hub, a Chilean type of hub...," Choquette said.
He stressed Methanex would only pursue projects that yielded sufficient returns in excess of its cost of capital.

The company's highest priority is strategic development of its business and beyond that, returning any excess cash to shareholders, Choquette said. The company has set an objective of keeping its debt at between 35 and 40 percent of its total capitalization.
Methanex also announced Thursday plans to buy back up to 10 percent of its shares and Choquette said this would not impair the company's ability to pursue new projects.
